notes.definition: Food security means having enough food to feed a population. Several biological factors threaten food security, so sustainable methods must be found to feed all the people on Earth.
explanation: Food security means having enough food to feed a population. A population is food secure when everyone can reliably get enough food. When there is not enough food, people suffer from hunger and malnutrition, and in the worst cases famine. The human population is still growing, so producing enough food is one of the biggest challenges the world faces.

The increasing birth rate has threatened food security in some countries. If the population grows faster than food production, there is less food available per person. At the same time, changing diets in developed countries mean that scarce food resources are transported around the world. For example, demand for foods such as exotic fruit, soya or meat can lead to land and water in poorer countries being used to grow food for export instead of food for local people.

New pests and pathogens can affect farming. A new disease or insect pest may spread into an area where the crops or livestock have no resistance to it, and destroy large amounts of food. Environmental changes can also affect food production. For example, widespread famine can occur in some countries if the rains fail, because crops cannot grow and animals cannot be fed without water.

The cost of agricultural inputs also matters. Inputs are the things farmers need, such as seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, animal feed, machinery and fuel. If these become more expensive, poorer farmers may not be able to afford them and crop yields fall. Conflicts that have arisen in some parts of the world can affect the availability of water or food, for example by destroying farms, stopping people farming, or blocking the transport of food.

Because of all these threats, sustainable methods must be found to feed all the people on Earth. Sustainable food production means producing enough food now without damaging the environment or using up resources, so that future generations can also produce enough food. Later subtopics look at some of these methods: efficient farming techniques, sustainable fisheries and biotechnology.
keyFacts: Food security means having enough food to feed a population.
An increasing birth rate has threatened food security in some countries.
Changing diets in developed countries mean scarce food resources are transported around the world.
New pests and pathogens can affect farming by destroying crops or livestock.
Environmental changes affect food production, e.g. famine if the rains fail.
The cost of agricultural inputs (seeds, fertiliser, feed, fuel) affects how much food can be produced.
Conflicts can affect the availability of water or food.
Sustainable methods must be found to feed all people on Earth.

keyTerms.definition: Having enough food to feed a population.
A severe, widespread shortage of food in an area, causing hunger and deaths.
A microorganism that causes disease, such as a fungus that infects crops.
An organism, often an insect, that damages crops or livestock and reduces food production.
Things farmers need to buy to produce food, such as seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, animal feed, machinery and fuel.
Producing enough food now in ways that do not damage the environment or use up resources, so future generations can also produce food.

workedExamples.title: Percentage increase in population
workedExamples.question: The population of a country increased from 40 million to 46 million. Calculate the percentage increase.

workedExamples.title: Food available per person
workedExamples.question: A country produces 9.0 million tonnes of grain for 30 million people. The population increases by 20% but grain production stays the same. Calculate the grain available per person before and after, and comment on food security.
steps: Less food is available per person, so food security has decreased.
workedExamples.answer: 0.30 tonnes per person before, 0.25 tonnes per person after: food security is reduced.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think food insecurity only happens because the world does not grow enough food in total.
misconceptions.right: In fact it also depends on who can get the food: conflict, high costs and food being transported to wealthier countries can leave some populations without enough food.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think changing diets only affect the people in developed countries.
misconceptions.right: In fact demand in developed countries means scarce food resources (and the land and water to grow them) are transported around the world, which can reduce food available in poorer countries.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a famine is caused only by people not working hard enough on farms.
misconceptions.right: In fact famine is usually caused by factors such as rains failing, new pests or pathogens, or conflict, which destroy crops or stop food reaching people.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think sustainable means 'producing as much as possible'.
misconceptions.right: In fact sustainable means producing enough food now without damaging the environment or resources, so that food can still be produced in the future.

realWorld: Fall armyworm, an insect pest from the Americas, reached Africa in 2016 and spread quickly, damaging maize crops on which many families depend.
Repeated failure of the seasonal rains in parts of East Africa has caused crop failures, livestock deaths and food shortages.
Rising prices of fertiliser and fuel make it harder for small farmers to buy inputs, reducing their harvests.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic (factors affecting food security) is in separate Biology (8461) only. It is not assessed in Combined Science Trilogy (8464).
examTips: Learn the six factors from the specification as a list: birth rate, changing diets, new pests and pathogens, environmental change, cost of inputs, conflict.
For 'explain' questions, link each factor to its effect on food: e.g. new pathogen → crops have no resistance → crops die → less food produced.
In data questions, compare the rate of population growth with the rate of food production to judge whether food security is improving or getting worse.
Use the precise definition: food security means having enough food to feed a population.
summary: Food security means having enough food to feed a population.
Increasing birth rate means more people to feed.
Changing diets in developed countries move scarce food resources around the world.
New pests and pathogens destroy crops and livestock.
Environmental changes such as failed rains can cause famine.
High costs of agricultural inputs and conflict reduce food availability.
Sustainable methods are needed to feed everyone, now and in the future.

questions.question: What does the term food security mean?
options: Keeping food locked away from pests
Making sure food is safe to eat
Having enough food to feed a population
Growing only one type of crop
markScheme: 1 mark: having enough food to feed a population
questions.explanation: Food security is about having enough food for a population. Food safety (food being safe to eat) is a different idea.

questions.question: Which of these is a biological factor that threatens food security?
options: New pests and pathogens that affect farming
Better storage of grain
Building more greenhouses
Using disease-resistant crops
markScheme: 1 mark: new pests and pathogens that affect farming
questions.explanation: New pests and pathogens can destroy crops and livestock. The other options would tend to improve food security.

questions.question: Widespread famine can occur in some countries when:
options: crops are grown in greenhouses
fishing quotas are introduced
the population falls
the rains fail
markScheme: 1 mark: the rains fail
questions.explanation: Without rain, crops cannot grow and livestock cannot be watered or fed, so food production collapses. A falling population would reduce demand for food.

questions.question: How do changing diets in developed countries affect food security?
options: They reduce the need for farming worldwide
Scarce food resources are transported around the world
They stop new pests from spreading
They lower the birth rate in poorer countries
markScheme: 1 mark: scarce food resources are transported around the world
questions.explanation: Demand from developed countries for a wider range of foods means scarce food (and the land and water used to grow it) is moved around the world, which can reduce food available locally.

questions.question: Why does an increasing birth rate threaten food security in some countries?
options: Babies eat more food than adults
It increases the cost of fertiliser
There are more people to feed, so food may not keep up with demand
It causes the rains to fail
markScheme: 1 mark: there are more people to feed, so food may not keep up with demand
questions.explanation: If the population grows faster than food production, there is less food per person.

questions.question: According to the specification, conflicts in some parts of the world threaten food security because they affect:
options: the availability of water or food
the number of trophic levels
the amount of light for photosynthesis
the size of fishing nets
markScheme: 1 mark: the availability of water or food
questions.explanation: Conflict can destroy farms and water supplies, stop people farming and block transport, so less water and food are available.

questions.question: The cost of fertiliser and fuel rises sharply. What is the most likely effect on food security in a poorer farming region?
options: Food security improves because farmers work harder
No effect, because fertiliser is not needed for crops
Food security improves because less fuel is used
Food security falls because farmers cannot afford inputs and yields drop
markScheme: 1 mark: food security falls because farmers cannot afford inputs and yields drop
questions.explanation: Fertiliser and fuel are agricultural inputs. If farmers cannot afford them, crops grow less well and less food is produced.

questions.question: Which statement best describes sustainable food production?
options: Producing as much food as possible this year, whatever the cost
Producing enough food now without damaging resources, so future generations can also produce food
Producing food only for export to developed countries
Producing food without using any farmland
markScheme: 1 mark: producing enough food now without damaging resources, so future generations can also produce food
questions.explanation: Sustainability is about meeting today's needs without reducing the ability to meet future needs. Maximum production at any cost could damage soil, water and wildlife.

questions.question: Which is an example of an environmental change that threatens food production?
options: A rise in the price of seeds
A war blocking roads to markets
Repeated droughts reducing crop yields in a region
People in another country choosing to eat more avocados
markScheme: 1 mark: repeated droughts reducing crop yields
questions.explanation: Drought is a change in the environment. Seed prices are the cost of agricultural inputs, war is conflict, and food choices abroad are changing diets: all threats, but not environmental changes.

questions.question: Which of these is an agricultural input?
options: Fertiliser
Rainfall
Harvested wheat
Famine
markScheme: 1 mark: fertiliser
questions.explanation: Agricultural inputs are things farmers buy to produce food, such as fertiliser, seeds and fuel. Rainfall is not bought, and harvested wheat is an output.

questions.question:
The population of a country increased from 40 million to 46 million.
Calculate the percentage increase in population.
markScheme: 1 mark: 15%
questions.explanation: Increase = 6 million. 6 ÷ 40 × 100 = 15%. Dividing by 46 instead of the original value (40) gives the wrong answer.

questions.question:
A farmer normally harvests 8.0 tonnes of maize per hectare. A new insect pest destroys 12% of the crop.
Calculate the yield the farmer now harvests per hectare.
markScheme: 1 mark: 7.04 tonnes per hectare
questions.explanation: 12% of 8.0 is 0.96 tonnes, so 8.0 − 0.96 = 7.04 tonnes per hectare remain.

questions.question:
A country produces 9.0 million tonnes of grain each year for a population of 30 million. The population increases by 20%, but grain production stays the same.
Calculate the mass of grain available per person after the increase.
markScheme: 1 mark: new population = 30 × 1.2 = 36 million
1 mark: 0.25 tonnes per person
questions.explanation: The population rises to 36 million, so each person has 9.0 ÷ 36 = 0.25 tonnes, down from 0.30 tonnes. This shows how a rising birth rate threatens food security.

questions.question:
A village normally harvests 500 tonnes of sorghum. In a year when the rains fail, the harvest is 350 tonnes.
Calculate how many tonnes less were harvested.
markScheme: 1 mark: 500 − 350 = 150 tonnes
questions.explanation: Subtract the drought harvest from the normal harvest: 500 − 350 = 150 tonnes.

questions.question:
A village normally harvests 500 tonnes of sorghum. In a year when the rains fail, the harvest is 350 tonnes.
Calculate the percentage decrease in the harvest.
markScheme: 1 mark: 30%
questions.explanation: Decrease = 150 tonnes. Percentage decrease = 150 ÷ 500 × 100 = 30%. Always divide by the original value.

questions.question: Define food security.
acceptedAnswers: having enough food to feed a population
markScheme: 1 mark: having enough food to feed a population
questions.explanation: This is the specification definition, so learn it word for word.

questions.question: Give two biological factors that threaten food security.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: increasing birth rate; changing diets in developed countries; new pests and pathogens; environmental changes such as rains failing; cost of agricultural inputs; conflicts affecting water or food
questions.explanation: Any two of the six factors listed in the specification score.

questions.question: State what can happen in some countries if the rains fail.
markScheme: 1 mark: (widespread) famine / crops fail
questions.explanation: Failed rains mean crops cannot grow, which can cause widespread famine.

questions.question: Explain how a new crop pathogen arriving in a country could threaten food security.
markScheme: 1 mark: crops have no resistance to the new pathogen / disease spreads quickly
1 mark: crops are damaged or die, so yield falls and less food is produced
questions.explanation: The key link is from disease to reduced yield. New pathogens are especially dangerous because local crops have not been bred to resist them.

questions.question: Explain how changing diets in developed countries can reduce food security in poorer countries.
markScheme: 1 mark: demand for a wider range of foods means scarce food resources are transported around the world
1 mark: land / water in poorer countries used to grow food for export, leaving less food for local people
questions.explanation: The specification phrase is that scarce food resources are transported around the world. Linking this to less food locally gives the second mark.

questions.question: Explain how conflict in a region can affect food security.
markScheme: 1 mark: conflict affects the availability of water or food
1 mark: e.g. farms or water supplies destroyed / people forced to leave their land / food transport blocked
questions.explanation: Conflict reduces both food production and the ability to move food to people who need it.

questions.question: Suggest why a rise in the cost of agricultural inputs has a greater effect on food security in poorer countries than in richer countries.
acceptedAnswers: richer countries can still buy inputs
markScheme: 1 mark: farmers in poorer countries have less money / cannot afford inputs such as fertiliser, seeds or fuel
1 mark: so they use fewer inputs and crop yields fall
1 mark: richer countries can still afford inputs (or import food), so their food production is less affected
questions.explanation: The same price rise is a much bigger share of a poor farmer's income, so it is more likely to reduce how much food they produce.

questions.question: Explain why sustainable methods must be found to feed all the people on Earth.
markScheme: 1 mark: the human population is increasing / more food is needed, but resources such as land, water and soil are limited
1 mark: methods must not damage the environment or use up resources, so food can still be produced in the future
questions.explanation: Unsustainable methods might increase food now but damage soils, water or fish stocks, reducing food production for future generations.

questions.question: Explain why an increasing birth rate has threatened food security in some countries.
acceptedAnswers: population grows faster than food production
markScheme: 1 mark: there are more people to feed
1 mark: if food production does not increase as fast, there is less food per person
questions.explanation: Food security depends on the balance between food produced and the number of people to feed.

questions.question:
Between 2000 and 2020, food production in a country increased by 25%, but its population increased by 40%.
Explain what has happened to food security in this country.
acceptedAnswers: population increased faster than food production
markScheme: 1 mark: the population increased faster than food production
1 mark: so there is less food per person / food security has decreased
questions.explanation: Even though more food is produced, it is shared among proportionally more people, so food per person has fallen.

questions.question: Describe and explain the biological factors that threaten food security around the world.
markScheme: Indicative content:
food security means having enough food to feed a population
increasing birth rate: more people to feed, food production may not keep up
changing diets in developed countries: scarce food resources transported around the world, land used to grow export crops
new pests and pathogens: spread to crops or livestock with no resistance, destroying food
environmental change: e.g. rains fail, drought, crops fail, widespread famine
cost of agricultural inputs: seeds, fertiliser, feed and fuel may be unaffordable, so yields fall
conflict: affects availability of water or food, farms destroyed, transport blocked
sustainable methods must be found to feed everyone
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): at least four factors described, each clearly explained in terms of the effect on food availability.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): several factors described with some explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two factors named with little or no explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: For top marks, cover a range of the six specification factors and say how each one reduces the amount of food available to people.

questions.question:
A country's population is increasing quickly, and its rainfall is becoming less reliable.
Explain how these two changes could affect food security in this country.
markScheme: Indicative content:
increasing population means more people to feed
more food needed; if production does not keep up, less food per person
less reliable rainfall means crops may fail / lower yields
livestock lack water and food
risk of widespread famine if the rains fail
together, demand rises while supply may fall, so food security decreases
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both changes clearly explained and linked to reduced food security.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one change explained, or both simply stated.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Good answers show that one factor increases demand for food while the other reduces supply, so together they strongly threaten food security.
